text: In 1920s Montreal a boy is being raised by two men who disagree about what a life is for: a grandfather who tells stories, a father who will not take a job. The scale stays domestic, a kitchen and a street and the gap between an adult's voice and a child's height. Of the honors this one collected, the screenplay prize is the telling one: the picture runs on talk, on what grown men say in front of a boy and what they say when they believe he is elsewhere. Ján Kadár made it in English, in Canada, in 1975, and gave it 102 unhurried minutes. The stakes are small and complete. A child is working out which of two men to believe, and that decision will fix, early and probably for good, what he is later prepared to call true.

Three families, one film, and no announced reason they belong in the same story. Kim Tae-yong runs the strands separately, each household keeping its own grievances, and the quarrels are the ordinary kind, the sort people have because they have run out of ways to say the other thing. Split three ways, 113 minutes gives each family about the span of a long short, so every argument has to land the first time and nobody gets a slow introduction. That is a gamble, and what it buys is comparison. Set the households beside one another and the resemblances start doing the work that explanation would otherwise have to do. It took the Grand Bell for best film and sits on the Korean Film Archive's hundred, which is substantial standing for a domestic drama of this size.

A woman in Busan is looking for a son she lost at Gilsodom, and by 1985 the war that took him is three decades gone. That interval is the film's real subject. A missing child stays a child in the mind of the person missing him, while elsewhere he has been aging into a life that may have no vacancy in it. Im Kwon-taek puts the pressure not on whether a search succeeds but on what a claim of blood is worth after thirty years of separate weather: whether a word like mother survives that much disuse, and what it obliges a stranger to do if it does. The Baeksang for best film went to it, and the Korean Film Archive keeps it among its hundred. 102 minutes, held to the size of one woman's errand.

An affair that begins at work has a schedule before it has anything else. Jang Sun-woo puts a runaway husband, the wife he brought with him, and a younger woman at the next machine in the same garment factory, in a place small enough that concealment becomes a second job. The wife is why this is not a romance. Her history arrives early and without pity, a stepmother she survived, years of housekeeping and bar work before she met him, then a child, so the man's new appetite is priced before it is indulged. It runs 114 minutes, took the Baeksang for best film and a place on the Korean Film Archive's hundred. The question kept in front of the whole thing is not who he wants, but what she has already paid to be standing where she stands.

The destination belongs to the one traveler who cannot say it out loud. Three people with almost no money set out to take a young woman home, and she is mute, so the two men escorting her have to read a purpose they will never hear stated: a student who has given up on his own life and has fallen for her, and a beggar with firm views on how to live one. That errand is generous and presumptuous at once, and Bae Chang-ho lets it stay both. The route crosses South Korea in 1984 at ground level, through the parts of a country only met without money, and the 112 minutes go to the getting there rather than the arrival. The Baeksang for best film went to it. What holds the three together is that each of them has, for the moment, somewhere to be.

A Chinese restaurant on the edge of town, a barbershop, a motel: three jobs, three friends, and no plan among them. Lee Jang-ho's attention in 1980 is on the service counter, who stands behind it, who walks up to it, and what the arrangement does to a young man's sense of what he is allowed to want. The romances sort themselves by address. One friend wants the woman at the hair salon, another the woman at the barbershop, and the third is caught between a factory worker and a girl from the good part of town, which is less a choice between people than a choice about which life to keep asking for. 113 minutes of shared drinks and each other's love stories, and not one of the three can say what he will be doing in a year. The film does not pretend that saying it would help.

The dead man was a photographer, and almost everything the film learns about him arrives secondhand, from people being asked questions. Two detectives do the asking: Kim Seung-ho's veteran, who has worked many of these, and Kim Seong-ok's younger, bookish partner, who prefers ideas. Between them a portrait assembles out of testimony that does not agree with itself, an oblique and talky way to build a crime picture, and the reason a 1968 South Korean investigation still has something to argue about. The interest is not in who did it. It is in how badly a life resists summary by the people who stood nearest to it. 103 minutes, filed under crime and adventure, and closer in practice to a run of interviews held by two men who each suspect the other of asking the wrong things.

Marriage as paperwork: a man without papers, a woman who has them, and a price agreed between them. Baek Ho-bin is in the United States illegally, wants money quickly, and has a pregnant wife in Korea waiting for the day he can send for her, so everything he does is arguably for her. That is the trap the film sets. The further he goes to keep the promise, the less the promise resembles anything she would recognize as kept. Bae Chang-ho declines to moralize over the arrangement, treating fraud as work with hours and risks like any other, and lets the distance between Los Angeles and a room in Korea do what a lecture would ruin. 108 minutes, and a Baeksang for best film. The wife is present for none of it. She is the reason given for all of it.

A newspaper needs the next installment, and the man who owes it cannot leave the house. He was disabled in the war; his wife, who once adored him, now takes care of him, and the distance between those two verbs is the film. Lee Man-hee allows himself 91 minutes, too few to waste, so the marriage moves in increments too small to announce themselves. When temptation arrives, the husband answers it with thanks rather than anger, and gratitude turns out to be the heavier instrument, since a man who has already forgiven is very hard to leave. The Grand Bell for best film went to it, and the Korean Film Archive keeps it among its hundred. What she decides is the last thing the picture surrenders, and it is in no hurry to get there.

A biography of a comedian whose act depended on nobody being certain it was an act is a contradiction before the first frame. Explain him and the work stops working; withhold and there is nothing for a film to hold. Miloš Forman took the problem anyway, and the honors that followed say where the weight landed: a Silver Bear for direction, a best film prize from the Broadcast Film Critics, best actor from the Boston critics, that last for a performance whose assignment is to impersonate a man who was himself permanently impersonating. Comedy, drama and history are all listed as genres, and the list is not confused, it is accurate. 118 minutes given to a career built out of provocations that worked only while nobody stepped in to explain them.

The western is French, which is the first useful thing to know about it. Jacques Audiard works in English, sets it in Oregon in 1851, and aims at the part of the frontier the genre usually files under scenery: chemistry. Hermann Kermit Warm is a prospector with a formula, which makes him property, and two hired killers are dispatched after him under a name, the Sisters brothers, that the film is content to let sound ridiculous. What the outsider's angle yields is the frontier as inconvenience: distances, expenses, bodies that do not hold up, work to be done again tomorrow. Violence is quick here and recovery from it is slow. 121 minutes, a Silver Lion for direction, and most of the comedy coming from men in the murder trade who are tired, unwell, and poor at conversation.

The trap closes early: a young officer is inside the wing when the riot starts, and his one route through the hour is to pass as an inmate. Everything after that is a performance carrying a fatal penalty for a dropped line, which is why the honors gather around acting and writing, best actor twice over and a European prize for the screenplay, rather than around scale. Daniel Monzón holds it to 108 minutes and mostly indoors, and the pressure is arithmetic: each additional man who learns the guard's name shortens his odds. The Spanish-language production, made out of France, took the Goya for best film. Under the mechanics sits a plainer question about how fast a person will learn the rules of a place built to look as though it had none.

A debt gets paid with a wedding, and neither of the people being married has been consulted. A small-time hustler owes a gangster more than he has; a teenage son is offered as currency; a daughter waits on the other side of the ledger; and the two young people at the center of the transaction have plans nobody senior has bothered to hear. Emir Kusturica runs it 127 minutes, long for a comedy, and the length is the method: the film keeps widening to admit more relatives, more claims, more competing schemes, until the wedding stops being an event and becomes a weather system with a date on it. The cinematography took a European Film Award, the direction a Silver Lion. Everything here is negotiable except the debt, the one thing all parties agree is real.

A reality show about surviving the apocalypse is shooting in West Virginia. The apocalypse is a set; the family in the woods is not. Joe Lynch takes the standard sequel assignment, the same backwoods cannibals and a fresh supply of visitors, and hands it a conceit that does more work than it strictly needs to: contestants already performing for cameras, already committed to staying where sensible people would leave, because leaving is losing. A retired colonel runs the game. The gore is why the film exists and it is not coy about that, delivered across 97 minutes without apology or ambition beyond the job. Nothing here argues for its own importance, which counts as a kind of manners. It was made to be watched late, loud, and in company.
